evidence.title: Inklings
evidence.text: The Inklings was an informal literary discussion group associated with the University of Oxford, England, for nearly two decades between the early 1930s and late 1949.

evidence.title: Inklings
evidence.text: The Inklings were literary enthusiasts who praised the value of narrative in fiction and encouraged the writing of fantasy.

evidence.title: Colin Hardie
evidence.text: Colin Graham Hardie (16 February 1906 – 17 October 1998) was a British classicist and academic.

evidence.title: Colin Hardie
evidence.text: From 1933 to 1936, he was Director of the British School at Rome.

evidence.title: Colin Hardie
evidence.text: From 1936 to 1973, he was a Fellow of Magdalen College, Oxford, and a tutor in classics.

evidence.title: Colin Hardie
evidence.text: In addition, from 1967 to 1973, he was the Public Orator of the University of Oxford.

evidence.title: Colin Hardie
evidence.text: He was a member of the Inklings, an informal literary discussion group which included the likes of J. R. R. Tolkien and C. S. Lewis.

evidence.title: Litbits
evidence.text: Litbits is a literary discussion radio programme and podcast, hosted by academic Adam Smyth and literary journalist James Kidd.

evidence.title: Litbits
evidence.text: Guests on the programme have included Polly Russell, Paul Myerscough, Alex von Tunzelmann, Samantha Ellis, Jonathan Beckman, Hallie Rubenhold, Steve Rose, Joe Brooker, Dennis Duncan, Dinah Roe, Giles Milton and Liane Strauss.

evidence.title: Litbits
evidence.text: Subjects covered include Rooms and Procrastination.

evidence.title: Eagle Street College
evidence.text: The Eagle Street College was an informal literary society established in 1885 at the home of James William Wallace in Eagle Street, Bolton, to read and discuss literary works, particularly the poetry of Walt Whitman, (1819–91).

evidence.title: Eagle Street College
evidence.text: The group subsequently became known as the Bolton Whitman Fellowship or Whitmanites.

evidence.title: Eagle Street College
evidence.text: Its founder members were Wallace, Dr John Johnston and Fred Wild.

evidence.title: Eagle Street College
evidence.text: The group held an annual 'Whitman Day' celebration around the 31 May which was the poet's birthday.

evidence.title: Petrashevsky Circle
evidence.text: The Petrashevsky Circle was a Russian literary discussion group of progressive-minded commoner-intellectuals in St. Petersburg in the 1840s.

evidence.title: Petrashevsky Circle
evidence.text: It was organized by Mikhail Petrashevsky, a follower of the French utopian socialist Charles Fourier.

evidence.title: Petrashevsky Circle
evidence.text: Among the members were writers, teachers, students, minor government officials, and army officers.

evidence.title: Petrashevsky Circle
evidence.text: While differing in political views, most of them were opponents of the tsarist autocracy and Russian serfdom.

evidence.title: Petrashevsky Circle
evidence.text: Like that of the Lyubomudry group founded earlier in the century, the purpose of the circle was to discuss Western philosophy and literature that was officially banned by the Imperial government of Tsar Nicholas I.

evidence.title: Charles Leslie Wrenn
evidence.text: Charles Leslie Wrenn (1895–1969) was a British scholar.

evidence.title: Charles Leslie Wrenn
evidence.text: He became Rawlinson and Bosworth Professor of Anglo-Saxon at the University of Oxford in 1945, the successor in the chair of J.R.R. Tolkien, and held the position until 1963.

evidence.title: Charles Leslie Wrenn
evidence.text: Wrenn was a Fellow of Pembroke College, Oxford.

evidence.title: Charles Leslie Wrenn
evidence.text: He was also a member of the Oxford literary discussion group known as the "Inklings", which included C. S. Lewis and Tolkien.

evidence.title: Charles Leslie Wrenn
evidence.text: Some of the work published by Wrenn includes "The English Language" (1949), "A Study of Old English Literature" (1967)"," and "An Old English Grammar," written with Randolph Quirk (1955, rev. 1957).

evidence.title: Charles Leslie Wrenn
evidence.text: His literary interests were primarily comparative literature and later poets including T. S. Elliot.

evidence.title: Adam Fox
evidence.text: Adam Fox (1883 – 1977), Canon, was the Dean of Divinity at Magdalen College, Oxford.

evidence.title: Adam Fox
evidence.text: He was one of the first members of the "Inklings", a literary group which also included C.S. Lewis and J.R.R. Tolkien.

evidence.title: Adam Fox
evidence.text: Between 1938 and 1942 he was Professor of Poetry.

evidence.title: Adam Fox
evidence.text: Later he became Canon of Westminster Abbey and he is buried there in Poet's Corner.

evidence.title: Adam Fox
evidence.text: He was also Warden (Headmaster) of the famous Radley College.

evidence.title: Nikolay Speshnev
evidence.text: Nikolay Alexandrovich Speshnev (Russian: Николай Александрович Спе́шнев; 1821, Kursk - 1882, St. Petersburg) was a 19th-century Russian aristocrat and political activist, best known for his involvement with the pro-socialist literary discussion group the Petrashevsky Circle.

evidence.title: Nikolay Speshnev
evidence.text: He formed a secret revolutionary society from among the members of the circle, which included the young Fyodor Dostoevsky.

evidence.title: Nikolay Speshnev
evidence.text: After the government of Tsar Nicholas I arrested the members of the Petrashevsky Circle in 1849, Speshnev was interrogated, threatened with torture, and eventually sentenced, along with Dostoevsky, Petrashevsky and others, to execution by firing squad.

evidence.title: Nikolay Speshnev
evidence.text: The sentence was commuted to hard labour in Siberia, but the prisoners were only informed of this after enduring a mock execution.

evidence.title: Roger Lancelyn Green
evidence.text: Roger (Gilbert) Lancelyn Green (2 November 1918 – 8 October 1987) was a British biographer and children's writer.

evidence.title: Roger Lancelyn Green
evidence.text: He was an Oxford academic who formed part of the Inklings literary discussion group along with C. S. Lewis and J. R. R. Tolkien.

evidence.title: Norma Guillard
evidence.text: Norma Guillard Limonta is a Cuban social psychologist and adjunct lecturer at the University of Havana.

evidence.title: Norma Guillard
evidence.text: She is a co-founder of Grupo Oremi, a now defunct lesbian discussion group in Cuba.

evidence.title: Norma Guillard
evidence.text: Her academic works borders on gender, sexuality, race and identity.

evidence.title: Norma Guillard
evidence.text: Guillard is a foundation member of the Cuban branch of La Articulacion Regional de Afrodescendientes de Latinoamerica y el Caribe, a joint regional discussion group composed of individuals of African descent in Latin America and the Caribbean.
